gold_label_note: Derived from Transcript A (strong hire, 48.5/50). Includes one deliberate miss-and-recover on hardware lead time (T7) so the judge learns recovery != penalty.

turns.text: Thanks for making time. Here's our situation: we've got 20 years of patient data in an on-prem SQL Server, and leadership wants to use your AI platform to predict 30-day readmission risk. Fair warning — we have zero cloud presence, extreme HIPAA constraints, our IT team is openly hostile to anything cloud-shaped, and all data has to stay within EU borders. Where would you start?

Before I design anything, can I ask three questions? First — you said HIPAA, but also EU data residency. Those don't normally coexist. Are you a US chain with EU hospitals, or an EU company where HIPAA is shorthand for strict health privacy? If you're EU, the operative regime is GDPR Article 9 special-category data, and your Data Protection Officer should be in the room from day one.
Honestly? Our CEO read that in an American article. We're a German company — 14 hospitals. GDPR is what our DPO, Frau Keller, cares about.

Good — then data stays in Germany, full stop, and I'll stop saying HIPAA because it would signal I haven't listened. Second: who's the sponsor and what's the business pain behind 'predict readmissions'? Bed capacity, quality metrics, payer negotiations? Third: what compute can you host — do you have spare virtualization capacity, or would we need to bring hardware inside your perimeter?
Sponsor is Dr. Weber, our Chief Medical Officer. Readmission rates are hurting our quality metrics and our payer negotiations. On compute — what were you assuming?

My default plan was to ship a pre-configured appliance into your data center in week one so we control the stack. Here's my 30 days in three parallel tracks: trust and governance, technical de-risking, problem formulation. And I want to set one expectation in minute five: day 30 is not a production model. It's a working prototype on your real data inside your own network, plus a costed go/no-go memo for Dr. Weber. Week one, the most important meeting is with your IT director — not to present an architecture at him, but to co-design it with him: nothing leaves your network, he specs the segmentation and access model, your team holds the keys. If IT co-owns the deployment, this survives; if we route around them, it dies in month three. Same week: kickoff with Dr. Weber on success criteria, and a session with Frau Keller to start the DPIA — automated risk scoring on health data at scale almost certainly requires one, and DPIAs have weeks of latency, so starting late is starting dead. I'd also want to identify a clinical champion, a discharge planner or hospitalist who'd actually change a decision based on the score.

One correction on the appliance idea. New physical hardware into our data center is six weeks minimum — procurement plus the change-management board. We do have maybe eight spare VMs on existing virtualization. Also, just so we're aligned: your sales team told us production model, live in our workflow, in 30 days. I've repeated that number to my board.

Then my plan as stated has a hole, and I'm glad it surfaced now. Scrap the appliance for phase one: the prototype runs on your existing VMs — eight is plenty for tabular modeling — while production hardware goes through procurement in parallel, starting week one so the six weeks overlaps the prototype instead of following it. The prototype environment and the production environment don't need to be the same box; they need to be inside the same trust boundary. On the sales promise — I'll be straight with you: a production model in a clinical workflow in 30 days would be reckless, and I'm going to have that conversation with our own account team, in writing, not make it your problem. But here's what I can put in front of your board instead: a live demo on your real data, inside your own data center, in 30 days — plus a production decision with a costed plan and dates attached. That's a stronger story than a rushed model that a clinician catches making a bad call in week six.
So I go back to my board with less than I promised them?

You go back with something true, dated, and demonstrable — 'we saw it run on our data in our building' beats 'it's in production' the first time someone asks a hard question. And the memo gives them the number they actually need: what production costs and when it lands. Now, the data itself. Twenty years is the headline, but twenty years of hospital data almost certainly spans an EHR migration, an ICD coding transition, probably an acquisition or two, and COVID distorted admission patterns. What's your history there?
You just described us. EHR migration in 2016, coding changed at that boundary, and we acquired two hospitals in 2019 that coded things their own way.

Then I would not train on all twenty years. Recent years for training, the most recent months held out for validation — a temporal split, never a random one, because a random split on longitudinal patient data leaks the same patient across train and test and inflates every metric you'd show Dr. Weber. The deep history I'd use only for patient-level features like long-run admission counts, where a little coding noise is tolerable. And before any model: the label needs negotiating with your clinical side — index admission definition, exclusions for planned readmissions like chemo cycles, transfers, in-hospital deaths, and the prediction time point, because 'at discharge' and '48 hours before discharge' see different data. Then a boring baseline first — a LACE-style score or logistic regression — so the story is lift over standard of care, not a naked number. For access, week one I'd ask for a pseudonymized extract into a sandbox inside your network.

I ran that access request past Frau Keller this morning. Her answer: no patient data — even pseudonymized — gets touched hands-on by anyone who isn't an employee. She's not being difficult; she's been burned. What's your plan that works with that?

Two moves, neither of which is arguing with her — in EU healthcare the DPO can veto this unilaterally, and being the vendor who respected that is worth more than three weeks of schedule. First: mediated access. I pair with your DBA and analysts; our platform runs, their hands are on the data, mine never are. Slower, but it builds internal ownership I want anyway. Second, in parallel: I build the whole pipeline — feature logic, label construction, evaluation harness — against your schema using synthetic data, so the day Frau Keller clears an access model, real data flows through a finished pipeline in days, not weeks. And the DPIA we started in week one is what eventually widens access for production.
OK. Say the model works. What am I actually showing Dr. Weber at day 30 — an accuracy number?

Not accuracy, and not AUROC either — neither tells a discharge planner anything. The demo answers her operational question: at your discharge-planning capacity — say your teams can give enhanced support to N patients a day — flagging the top N by risk gets you this precision, meaning this many true readmissions caught that you currently miss. Plus calibration, because clinicians stop trusting a score the first time 80% turns out to mean 40%. To get N right, I'd want one shadowing session with a discharge planner in week one — thirty minutes watching how they work changes what the demo shows. Two more things go in the day-30 memo whether or not anyone asks. The EU AI Act: healthcare risk scoring plausibly classifies as high-risk, which means risk management, logging, human oversight, documentation — I'm not a lawyer, so the memo says engage counsel on classification now, but I'd architect for it regardless: decision support with a documented human in the loop, every prediction logged with feature-level attributions, an explicit override path. And fairness: before go-live we slice performance by age, sex, and socioeconomic proxies, because readmission models have a documented failure mode — populations who historically couldn't get readmitted look low-risk to the model, so acting on it withholds discharge support from exactly the people who need it most. That check costs a day in week four and costs you the program if it surfaces in month twelve.
Frau Keller will love that you said that unprompted. Anything else before we wrap?

Just the summary you can forward. Day 30 deliverables: platform running on your VMs inside your network with zero egress; baseline plus one gradient-boosted model on a temporal holdout, built through mediated access; a demo for Dr. Weber framed in catches-per-day at planner capacity; and a decision memo covering production hardware cost and lead time, DPIA status, AI Act classification next steps, and the fairness audit plan. Long-lead items — DPIA, procurement, and my conversation with our own sales team — all start this week, because they're the things that can't be compressed later.
